\title{Which Parts of BM25 Help Learned Top-$k$ Selection?\\
Tests in Sparse Retrieval, KV-Cache Page Selection and Expert Routing}

\begin{abstract}
BM25 corrects a term-match score with inverse document frequency (IDF), saturation and
length normalisation. We test which parts help three learned top-$k$ selectors that use
none of them, in sparse retrieval, KV-cache page selection and mixture-of-experts routing.
On thirteen collections, with fourteen sparse codes from one dense encoder, the full
correction raises mean nDCG@10 from $0.036$ to $0.158$. Saturation, which needs no
collection statistics, gives $62\%$ of this gain and IDF $10\%$, and in tests fixed in
advance the spread of a code's stored values ranks saturation's effect. The Zipf-like
frequency curve credited by prior work does not predict the gain, and agreement with text
BM25 is not a reliable label-free test of whether IDF and length normalisation help. In KV
selection and routing, where an item's frequency is its own selection rate, saturation and
length change mean accuracy by at most $0.02$, but IDF lowers mean RULER accuracy below $0.05$ on two
models and OLMoE's MMLU accuracy by $0.09$ to $0.10$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

BM25 scores a document by its term matches with the query, with three corrections to the
raw score \citep{sparckjones1972idf,robertson2009bm25}. Inverse document frequency (IDF)
gives little weight to a term that occurs in most documents. Saturation limits the reward
for repetition. In a document of average length, with BM25's usual $k_1 = 1.2$, a term
that occurs ten times scores only a quarter more than one that occurs three times. Length
normalisation discounts long documents, which match more terms by chance.

Three learned components of NLP systems keep the top $k$ items by a score and use none of
these corrections. A learned sparse retriever scores a document by an inner product of
non-negative query and document features and returns the top $k$
\citep{formal2021splade,nguyen2023unified}. Quest, a sparse-attention method, scores
fixed-size pages of the key-value (KV) cache against the current query and attends only to
the highest-scoring pages \citep{tang2024quest}. A mixture-of-experts router scores every
expert for a token and sends the token to the top $k$ \citep{shazeer2017moe,fedus2022switch}.
In each the score is non-negative or can be made so, and each item can be given a
frequency, so BM25's correction applies to all three (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}).

Applied to learned features, BM25 has both helped and hurt. On one benchmark suite it
beats the inner product by $0.20$ nDCG@10 on sparse-autoencoder features and loses by
$0.11$ on SPLADE-v3 \citep{clavie2026latent}. The explanation offered is that BM25 helps
when the features' document frequencies follow a Zipf-like curve, as word frequencies do
\citep{clavie2026latent,han2026bm25v}. If that is right, statistics of the frequency curve
should predict the sign of the gain before the experiment is run.

We test which parts of the correction help, and whether the gain can be predicted before
it is measured, in all three settings. In retrieval we hold the encoder fixed and vary only
the sparse code built on it. Fourteen codes come from one dense encoder, multilingual
E5-base, and each is scored on thirteen collections with each part switched on or off,
eight configurations in all. Exact Shapley values split each gain among the parts. A
frequency-curve predictor estimates the gain, and a label-free rule predicts from
agreement with a reference ranker whether IDF and length normalisation help. We fixed the main tests, and
any pass marks, before reading their results, and call them registered
(Table~\ref{tab:registered} in the appendix); the other analyses are exploratory.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The correction raises the E5 codes' mean nDCG@10 over the 182 code--collection pairs
from $0.036$ to $0.158$. On six collections the best code under the correction beats text
BM25 (Section~\ref{sec:helps}).
\item Saturation gives most of the gain ($62\%$) and IDF the least ($10\%$). Saturation
needs no collection statistics, and in registered tests the spread of the values stored in
the index ranks the size of its effect at held-out values of $k_1$
(Sections~\ref{sec:attribution} and~\ref{sec:mechanism}).
\item Statistics of the frequency curve do not predict the gain (Section~\ref{sec:curve}).
Fitted models that use agreement with text BM25 explain about half the held-out variance of
the gain from IDF and length normalisation, but the label-free rule based on that agreement
is no better in sign than a constant on 84 later rows and fails its registered test on SPLADE-v3
(Sections~\ref{sec:proxy} and~\ref{sec:splade}).
\item In KV selection and routing, with frequency counted from the selector's own choices,
IDF lowers RULER accuracy to near zero on two models and MMLU accuracy by $0.09$ to $0.10$,
and the frequency-curve predictor fails every registered test. With IDF off, saturation
provably cannot change these selections, up to ties. In KV selection, exact attention mass
shows the harm of IDF without labels. The registered rule built on it matches an oracle
but fails its sign test on both models, because adding IDF and length helps on no row and a constant
does as well (Sections~\ref{sec:transfer-method} and~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Term weighting and learned sparse retrieval.} IDF began as a statistical account
of term specificity \citep{sparckjones1972idf}. Saturation approximates the two-Poisson
model of within-document frequency \citep{robertson1994poisson}, and pivoted length
normalisation keeps long documents from being favoured or penalised
\citep{singhal1996pivoted}. BM25 combines the three \citep{robertson2009bm25}. Learned
sparse retrievers learn term weights through contextual exact match \citep{gao2021coil}
or vocabulary expansion \citep{formal2021splade,formal2021spladev2,lassance2024spladev3}.

\paragraph{BM25 on learned features.} Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense
activations into many non-negative features \citep{cunningham2024sae,gao2025topksae}.
\citet{clavie2026latent} score SAE features of a frozen dense retriever with BM25 and
report $0.582$ nDCG@10 against $0.381$ for the inner product, and the reverse on SPLADE-v3,
$0.455$ against $0.568$. CL-SR loses 11 to $18\%$ of its nDCG@10 on TREC-DL without IDF
\citep{park2025clsr}. \citet{han2026bm25v} find BM25 and the inner product about equal on
image features and credit top-$k$ filtering for suppressing what IDF would down-weight.
None of these varies the representation systematically or separates all three parts. We
hold the encoder fixed, derive fourteen codes from it and switch each part on and off, so
the gain can be split among the parts and set against properties of each code.

\paragraph{Predicting effectiveness without labels.} Query performance prediction estimates
retrieval quality from the query and the ranking
\citep{carmel2010difficulty,cronen2002clarity,shtok2012nqc}, and systems can be ranked
against pseudo-relevant documents \citep{soboroff2001ranking}. Our target, the
difference between two scorers, is new.

\paragraph{Selection inside the transformer.} Quest scores KV pages against page min-max key
summaries \citep{tang2024quest}. H2O keeps recent tokens and heavy hitters, the tokens that
have received the most attention \citep{zhang2023h2o}. SnapKV keeps the positions recent
queries attend to \citep{li2024snapkv}, StreamingLLM the first tokens and a recent window
\citep{xiao2024streamingllm}, and Expected Attention the positions future queries are
predicted to attend to \citep{devoto2025expectedattention}. Mixture-of-experts layers route
each token to its top-$k$ experts \citep{shazeer2017moe,lepikhin2021gshard,fedus2022switch},
balanced by an auxiliary loss \citep{zoph2022stmoe} or a load-driven bias
\citep{wang2024lossfree}, whose analogue we run as a baseline. H2O's heavy-hitter rule is
the opposite of IDF when frequency is a selection rate. A
load-driven bias moves tokens towards under-used experts, the same direction as IDF, but adds a
term to the router's score instead of multiplying it. We know of no work that applies
BM25's parts to KV selection or routing.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:problem}

\subsection{BM25's correction as three switches}

For query and document vectors $x_q$ and $x_d$ with non-negative coordinates (features),
we score
\begin{equation}
S(q,d) = \sum_{j} x_{qj}\, w_j\, T(x_{dj}, \ell_d),
\label{eq:scorer}
\end{equation}
and call $x_{dj}$ the stored value of feature $j$ in document $d$. Each part can be
switched on or off. With IDF on, the weight $w_j$ is
$\idf_j = \ln(1 + (N - df_j + 0.5)/(df_j + 0.5))$, where feature $j$ is nonzero in $df_j$
of the $N$ documents, and with IDF off $w_j = 1$. With saturation on, the transform is
$T(f,\ell) = (k_1+1)f/(f + k_1\ell)$, and with it off $T(f,\ell) = f/\ell$. With length
normalisation on, $\ell_d = 1 - b + b L_d/\overline{L}$, where $L_d = \sum_j x_{dj}$ is
the document's length and $\overline{L}$ its mean over the collection, and with it off
$\ell_d = 1$. We use BM25's usual $k_1 = 1.2$ and $b = 0.75$ unless stated.

We write a configuration as three bits in the order IDF, saturation, length. Configuration
\texttt{000} (all-off) is the plain inner product, \texttt{111} (all-on) is BM25, and
\texttt{010} is saturation alone. IDF and length normalisation need collection statistics
(document frequencies and mean length), while saturation uses only the document's own
values.

\subsection{Measuring each part's share of the gain}

A row is one sparse code on one collection at one setting of the support budget (a cap on
the number of nonzero features per query and per document), $k_1$, $b$ and the seed used to
fit the code. It carries eight nDCG@10 values $Q_c$, one per configuration $c$. The 182
primary rows are the fourteen codes on the thirteen collections at the default settings.

The gain of the full correction is $Q_{111} - Q_{000}$, and we split it among the parts by
Shapley values \citep{shapley1953value}. The Shapley value $\phi_s$ of part $s$ is the
change in nDCG@10 when $s$ is switched on, averaged over the six orders in which the three
parts can be switched on. Writing $Q_A$ for the configuration with the parts in $A$ on,
\begin{equation}
\phi_s = \sum_{A \not\ni s}
\tfrac{|A|!\,(2-|A|)!}{6}\bigl(Q_{A\cup\{s\}} - Q_{A}\bigr),
\label{eq:shapley}
\end{equation}
and the three values sum to the gain.

\subsection{Predicting the gain without measuring it}
\label{sec:predictors}

We predict two quantities. The frequency-curve predictor predicts the full gain, scaled as
the margin $m$ below. The label-free rule predicts the sign of $G = Q_{111} - Q_{010}$, the
gain from adding IDF and length normalisation once saturation is on. The sign of $G$ thus
decides whether collection statistics are worth computing.

\paragraph{The frequency-curve predictor.} Our project proposal planned a predictor of the
gain from the shape of the feature-frequency curve, as prior work implies, and we
fixed it before any retrieval result existed. It is a ridge
regression on three statistics of the curve (the Zipf slope, the variance of IDF and the
share of activations in the most frequent $1\%$ of features). Its target is the margin
$m = (Q_{111} - Q_{000})/\operatorname{sd}(Q_{000}, \ldots, Q_{111})$, the gain divided by
the spread of the eight scores, so that rows of different difficulty share one scale. The
margin is undefined in the three primary rows where all eight scores are equal.

\paragraph{The label-free rule.} Without relevance labels, each configuration's ranking can
still be compared with a reference ranker. We count the reference's top 10 for each query
as relevant and score each configuration against these pseudo-labels by nDCG@10, giving a
pseudo-quality $\tilde{Q}_c$. Putting $\tilde{Q}$ in place of $Q$ gives an estimate
$\tilde{G}$ of $G$ with no fitted parameter. The rule uses \texttt{111}
where $\tilde{G} > 0$ and \texttt{010} otherwise. In retrieval the registered reference is
text BM25, and the dense encoder E5, alone or fused with text BM25 by reciprocal rank, is a
secondary reference. In KV selection $\tilde{Q}_c$ is the exact attention mass of $c$'s
pages (Section~\ref{sec:setup}), with token F1 to the full-attention output as a secondary
measure.

\paragraph{Pass marks.} The label-free rule passes if its sign is right on more rows than
the better constant (the better of always predicting a gain and always predicting a loss)
and its choices score at least as well as all-on on average. We also
compare it with always choosing \texttt{010} and with an oracle that picks the better of
\texttt{111} and \texttt{010} in each row. Outside retrieval the
frequency-curve predictor must get the sign right on at least $0.70$ of rows, keep its mean
absolute error (MAE) on $m$ within $1.81$ ($1.5$ times its root mean squared error in retrieval), and beat always
predicting a gain, the majority sign in retrieval.

\subsection{Applying the correction to KV pages and experts}
\label{sec:transfer-method}

Eq.~\eqref{eq:scorer} applies to any selection with a non-negative score per item and a
frequency count. A KV page or an expert carries one score, so the sum has a single term.

\paragraph{KV pages.} Each page $i$ of 16 cached tokens in an attention head is one item.
To count frequencies, we run Quest at 64 positions of the example's own prompt
(calibration). A page's value $f_i$ is Quest's criticality, an upper bound on the
query--key product from the page's key minima and maxima, passed through a softplus and
divided by the head's median selected value during calibration. For page $i$, $N$ counts
the calibration positions at or after it, and $df_i$ those at which Quest selects it. The page's length is the
norm of its concatenated key minima and maxima.

\paragraph{Experts.} For expert $e$ the value is the router probability, the frequency is
the share of calibration tokens routed to $e$, and the length is the norm of the token's
router logits, which all experts of a token share. The selected experts keep their
original gate weights.

In both settings an item's frequency is the selector's own selection rate, so IDF gives low
weight to the items the selector picks often, and IDF's effect here partly follows from
this definition.

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:single}
When each item carries a single score $f_i \ge 0$, as a KV page or an expert does, and IDF
is off, the saturated score is a strictly increasing function of $f_i/\ell_i$ and selects
the same top $k$ as the unsaturated score, up to ties.
\end{proposition}

It holds because $(k_1+1)f/(f+k_1\ell) = g(f/\ell)$ with $g(f) = (k_1+1)f/(f+k_1)$, and $g$
is strictly increasing on $f \ge 0$. With IDF on, $\idf_i\,g(f_i)$ and $\idf_i f_i$ can
order items differently. In KV selection pages differ in length, so \texttt{001} can differ
from \texttt{000}, but \texttt{010} selects as \texttt{000} does and \texttt{011} as
\texttt{001}. In routing all experts of a token share one length, so the four
configurations with IDF off route identically up to ties, as do \texttt{100} and
\texttt{101}.

A row is one RULER task at one token budget in KV selection, and WikiText or one MMLU
subject in routing. The frequency-curve predictor is applied without refitting.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Sparse codes.} All retrieval codes come from
\texttt{multilingual-e5-base} (E5, \citealp{wang2024me5}) at a pinned revision. Seven
bases map an E5 state to a non-negative sparse vector. They are the identity, a Gaussian
projection to 768 dimensions and PCA to 384, each split into positive and negative parts;
soft $k$-means over $4{,}096$ centroids; product and residual quantisation (PQ, RQ; $8 \times 256$,
\citealp{jegou2011pq,chen2010rq}); and a Top-$K$ SAE with $8{,}192$ features of which at
most 32 are active. All but the identity are fitted on the same $200{,}000$ MS~MARCO
passages \citep{bajaj2016msmarco}. The bases form four families for held-out validation
(linear, clustered, quantised and learned). A basis is applied either to the mean of the
token states (pooled) or to each token state before summing (token), and each basis at one
granularity is one sparse code. The primary support budget keeps at most 32
nonzero features per query and 128 per document, and document frequencies, lengths and IDF
come from these capped vectors in each corpus. Retrieval is exact over the whole corpus.

\paragraph{Collections and sweeps.} The thirteen collections come from eleven corpora. They
are MS~MARCO dev with TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 on the same documents, six BEIR sets
\citep{thakur2021beir}, LIMIT \citep{weller2025limit} and the Hindi, Bengali and Telugu
portions of MIRACL \citep{zhang2023miracl}. Beyond the primary rows, sweeps vary one
setting each (Table~\ref{tab:families} in the appendix). SPLADE-v3
\citep{lassance2024spladev3}, with its own backbone, is scored under the same eight
configurations as an external comparison.

\paragraph{Significance.} All-on is compared with all-off by a paired bootstrap of
$Q_{111} - Q_{000}$ over queries or examples ($10{,}000$ draws; $2{,}000$ for SPLADE-v3 and
the transfer settings), with Holm's correction within each group of rows declared in
advance \citep{holm1979}.

\paragraph{KV-page selection.} The attention model is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
\citep{qwen2025qwen25} in float16, chosen before any run, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct is run
with the same protocol as a registered replication. All 13 tasks of the RULER
long-context benchmark \citep{hsieh2024ruler}, from needle retrieval to QA, are run at a 4K
context with 100 examples per task and token budgets of 512 and 1{,}024 over 16-token
pages. Prefill is dense and decoding attends only to the selected pages. Full attention,
Quest and H2O \citep{zhang2023h2o} are run beside the eight configurations. Configuration
\texttt{000} is Quest's scoring, and the softplus and per-head scaling keep Quest's order. The label-free reference is exact attention mass, the
share of full attention's softmax mass that falls on the pages a configuration would
select, measured along the full-attention generation.

\paragraph{Expert routing.} OLMoE-1B-7B \citep{muennighoff2025olmoe} routes each token to 8
of 64 experts. Quality is the mean token log-likelihood on WikiText-2
\citep{merity2017wikitext} in 2{,}048-token windows, reported as perplexity, and zero-shot
accuracy on each of the 57 MMLU subjects \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}, scored by the
likelihood of each choice. Frequencies come from 256 training-split windows for WikiText
and from each subject's own prompts for MMLU. A load-driven frequency bias, the analogue of
loss-free balancing \citep{wang2024lossfree}, is run beside the eight configurations.

\subsection{The correction raises the codes' nDCG@10}
\label{sec:helps}

Under the inner product the sparse codes are weak. Their
mean nDCG@10 is at most $0.135$ on every collection (Table~\ref{tab:quality}) and $0.036$
over the 182 primary rows. The full correction raises it on every collection, to $0.158$
over the primary rows. All-on beats all-off in 162 of the 182 primary rows, significantly
after Holm correction in 134. On six collections the best code under all-on beats text
BM25, three of them on the MS~MARCO corpus, two from MIRACL, and FiQA. The best code is the
token-level SAE on every collection but LIMIT. No code beats dense E5 except on
LIMIT, where E5 scores $0.015$ and only token-level $k$-means exceeds it ($0.033$).

In 81 rows the inner product scores below $0.01$, so nearly any correction beats it. All-on is also not the best configuration. It is the strict best of
the eight in only 42 rows, and \texttt{011} (saturation and length without IDF) has a
higher mean, $0.163$ against $0.158$, though not at the 16/64 budget ($0.101$ against $0.104$).

\subsection{Saturation gives most of the gain}
\label{sec:attribution}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2.4pt}
\input{tables/tab_shapley}
\caption{Mean Shapley value of each part (Eq.~\eqref{eq:shapley}) and their sum
$Q_{111} - Q_{000}$, in each setting's metric (nDCG@10 in retrieval, accuracy in KV
selection and MMLU, log-likelihood per token on WikiText). 16/64 and 64/256 are the
query and document support caps of the other budgets, and native is uncapped.}
\label{tab:shapley}
\end{table}

Saturation has the largest Shapley value at every support budget (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}).
Over the 182 primary rows it gives $62\%$ of the gain, length normalisation $28\%$ and IDF,
the part prior work credits, $10\%$. The two parts that need collection
statistics give $38\%$ ($95\%$ interval $36$ to $41\%$, resampling collections). Saturation alone (\texttt{010}) raises mean nDCG@10
from $0.036$ to $0.137$. As the budget grows, IDF's share shrinks and length's grows, and with uncapped (native) support
IDF's mean Shapley value is slightly negative. \citet{han2026bm25v} report the same trend
for image features, where document frequencies become more alike as more features are active.
Shuffling the frequencies turns IDF's Shapley value negative, but removing IDF from all-on
does not lower mean nDCG@10, over the primary rows (\texttt{011} scores $0.163$) or with
uniform frequencies on three collections (Appendix~\ref{app:bases}).

\figkvllamaoff
\figkvqwenon
\figkvllamaon
\legend{{Qwen, no IDF},{Llama, no IDF},{Qwen, IDF},{Llama, IDF}}
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Left, the spread of the stored values against saturation's Shapley value, one
point per primary retrieval row. Right, the share of full attention's mass on the selected
pages against RULER accuracy, one point per KV row and configuration with a mass
reference.}
\label{fig:panels}
\end{figure}

With length normalisation off, saturation maps a stored value $f$ to
$g(f) = (k_1+1)f/(f+k_1)$, and the ratio $g(f)/f$ falls as $f$ grows, so large values are
shrunk more than small ones. If every stored value in an index were equal, $g$ would
multiply every score by one factor and the ranking would not change. Pooled PQ and RQ are
such codes, with one active feature of value one per sub-quantiser or stage, and their
saturation and length effects are exactly zero in every row (Table~\ref{tab:bases} in the
appendix). The more unequal the values, the more saturation can reorder a ranking. We
measure this inequality by the coefficient of variation $\mathrm{cv}_x$ of the nonzero
values stored in the index. In our codes the reordering usually helps
($\phi_{\mathrm{sat}} > 0$ in $79\%$ of primary rows), and it grows with $\mathrm{cv}_x$
(Spearman $0.78$, Figure~\ref{fig:panels}, left).

We fixed six hypotheses on this mechanism in advance and tested them on the $k_1$ and $b$
sweep of five collections, mostly new rows (Table~\ref{tab:confirm} in the
appendix). All six pass. H2 predicts that a smaller $k_1$ gives a larger
$\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$, H3 that $\mathrm{cv}_x$ and $\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ correlate within a
corpus, and H6 that a larger $b$ gives a larger length effect. H5 (no length effect at $b = 0$) checks the implementation, and H1 and one arm of H6
reuse primary rows. In H4 a ridge model of
$\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ on $\mathrm{cv}_x$ fitted at $k_1 = 1.2$ ranks the rows by
$\phi_{\mathrm{sat}}$ at $k_1 = 0.6$ and $2.4$ (Spearman $0.87$, $0.90$).

\subsection{The frequency curve does not predict the gain}
\label{sec:curve}

The frequency-curve predictor explains almost none of the held-out variance of $m$, with
$R^2$ of $0.04$ when a basis family is held out and $0.02$ when a corpus is held out. Its
sign is right on $0.90$ of rows, no more often than always predicting a gain. Part of the
failure lies in the target. Of the margins, $85\%$ fall between $1.5$ and $3.5$, because in
many rows $Q_{000}$ is near zero and every other configuration is far above it, so $m$
reflects that pattern more than the size of the gain.

We also fitted exploratory ridge models of each Shapley value and of $G$ directly, on three
nested feature sets (Table~\ref{tab:predictor} in the appendix). The first holds the three
frequency-curve statistics. The second adds index statistics, which describe the nonzero
values stored in the index, chiefly $\mathrm{cv}_x$. The third adds the pseudo-qualities of
Section~\ref{sec:predictors} and features of each configuration's top-100 ranking. Index
statistics predict saturation's Shapley value (held-out $R^2$ of $0.29$ to $0.56$) but
predict $G$ no better than the frequency curve does ($0.01$ to $0.12$ against $0.01$ to
$0.13$). $G$ varies even within a code. For token-level SAE and PCA, the two strongest codes,
$G > 0$ on 6 of 13 collections.

\subsection{Agreement with text BM25 in place of labels}
\label{sec:proxy}

With pseudo-labels from text BM25 added, the fitted models reach positive held-out $R^2$ on
every target and every split, and for $G$ they reach $0.44$ to $0.59$, against at most
$0.13$ without pseudo-labels (Table~\ref{tab:predictor}). Within a row the pseudo-qualities order the eight
configurations almost as the true scores do (median Spearman $0.98$). The label-free rule was designed on the primary rows. On the 181 of them used in the fitted
models, all-on averages $0.1590$, the rule $0.1628$ and the oracle $0.1654$, so the rule
recovers $59\%$ of the gap to the oracle.

Our interim report stated the rule, unregistered, before we produced 84 new rows,
the fourteen codes at the 16/64 and 64/256 budgets on the three MS~MARCO collections.
All-on and the oracle are close on these rows ($0.202$ and $0.203$). With the text BM25 reference,
$\tilde{G}$ tracks $G$ (Spearman $0.91$), but its sign is right on $0.87$ of rows, against
$0.88$ for always predicting a gain. The dense or fused reference gets the sign right on
$0.95$, but the dense reference is the encoder the codes come from. The three collections
share one corpus, so these rows are not independent.

\section{The Correction on SPLADE-v3}
\label{sec:splade}

On SPLADE-v3 the correction costs a little, all of it through length normalisation, and
the label-free rule with the text BM25 reference fails. Mean nDCG@10 falls from $0.523$
under the inner product to $0.509$ under all-on, and falls on 8 of 10 collections
(Table~\ref{tab:quality}). All-on is significantly worse on 4 collections and
significantly better on ArguAna and LIMIT (bootstrap $p < 0.05$, uncorrected). The
direction matches the reversal of \citet{clavie2026latent}; the size, $0.013$ against their
$0.113$, does not. Without length normalisation, IDF and saturation (\texttt{110}) score
$0.528$, above the inner product (Appendix~\ref{app:bases}).

The SPLADE-v3 scores were known before this test was fixed, but the label-free estimates were not. The sign of $G$ splits 5 to 5, so a constant sign
scores only $0.50$. With the registered text BM25 reference, $\tilde{G}$ has the right sign
on 5 of 10 collections and Spearman $-0.04$ with $G$. On the three MS~MARCO
collections, adding IDF and length normalisation raises agreement with text BM25 by $0.06$
to $0.08$ while lowering nDCG@10. Configurations that behave like BM25 agree more with text
BM25, a bias noted in advance. The secondary dense reference meets both
pass marks. Its sign is right on 7 of 10 collections, and its rule scores $0.519$, against
$0.509$ for all-on and $0.515$ for \texttt{010}. Over 10 collections the $95\%$
interval for its gain over all-on includes zero. The fused reference fails.

\section{Transfer to KV Pages and Experts}
\label{sec:transfer}

\subsection{KV-page selection}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\input{tables/tab_attention}
\caption{Mean RULER accuracy (13 tasks, 4K context, 100 examples each) and mean share of
full attention's softmax mass on the pages each configuration would select, at token
budgets of 512 and 1{,}024. Full is full attention, and Quest equals \texttt{000} on every
example. Llama's mass covers the 938 of $1{,}300$ examples where full attention gives a non-empty
answer.}
\label{tab:attention}
\end{table*}

Without IDF the corrected selectors match Quest, and with IDF they fail. On Qwen the four
configurations without IDF stay within $0.02$ of Quest's mean accuracy ($0.71$ and $0.78$
at the two budgets), and the four with IDF score $0.015$ to $0.046$
(Table~\ref{tab:attention}). Variable tracking, run without RULER's answer prefix, scores
zero on Qwen, so its two rows have no defined margin. After
Holm correction all-on is significantly worse than all-off in all 24 remaining rows and
better in none, and $G$ is negative in all 24. The mean Shapley value of IDF is $-0.775$,
against $-0.003$ for saturation and $0.002$ for length (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}).

The replication on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct shows the same pattern. With IDF on,
mean accuracy is at most $0.002$, against $0.43$ and $0.46$ for Quest, and without IDF it
stays within $0.02$ of Quest. Three rows score zero in every configuration. In the other
23, all-on is significantly worse than all-off in 18 after Holm correction and better in
none, and IDF's mean Shapley value is $-0.509$.

IDF gives low weights to the pages Quest selects often. A page selected at all 64 calibration positions gets the smoothed
IDF $\ln(1 + 0.5/64.5) \approx 0.008$, and one never selected gets $\ln 130 \approx 4.9$.
On the first single-needle task with Qwen at the 1{,}024 budget, the page holding the
needle ranks between second and tenth of 210 to 247 pages by selection rate, so IDF gives
it a low weight. Averaged over tasks, the pages a configuration with IDF would
select hold $0.29$ to $0.44$ of the softmax mass on Qwen and $0.21$ to $0.32$ on Llama,
against $0.90$ to $0.95$ without IDF. On every task with a mass reference, each
configuration with IDF holds less mass than any configuration without
(Figure~\ref{fig:panels}, right).

As Proposition~\ref{prop:single} predicts, saturation without IDF changes task scores
almost nowhere. On Qwen, \texttt{010} and \texttt{000} differ in task score on 38 of
$2{,}600$ example--budget pairs and in token F1 to the full-attention output on 448, which we attribute to
floating-point ties.

The registered frequency-curve predictor fails on both models. On Qwen it predicts a gain
on all 24 rows and is wrong on every one, with an MAE of $4.18$ against the limit of
$1.81$. On Llama it is wrong on every row with a nonzero margin, with an MAE of $4.00$. Its
predictions on Qwen lie between $2.13$ and $2.21$, a gain for nearly any input, so this
failure is weak evidence about page frequency.

With exact attention mass as $\tilde{Q}$, the registered label-free rule chooses
\texttt{010} on every row where the reference exists (26 on Qwen, 24 on Llama), since the
pages chosen with IDF always hold less mass. On the rows with $G \ne 0$ (24 and 22) its
sign is always right, and its choices reach the oracle's mean accuracy ($0.742$ over the 26
Qwen rows and $0.484$ over the 24 Llama rows), against $0.024$ and $0.001$ for all-on.
Always choosing \texttt{010} does exactly as well, so these rows cannot show that the rule
adds anything over a constant. The registered test fails on the sign mark. No row has
$G > 0$, so always predicting a loss is also right on every row, and the pass mark requires
exceeding it. Across rows,
$\tilde{G}$ and $G$ have Spearman $-0.32$ on Qwen and $-0.03$ on Llama, so $\tilde{G}$ gets
the direction but not the size. Token F1 to full attention's output, the secondary
reference, gives the same decisions.

\subsection{Expert routing}

In routing IDF also hurts, by less. Configuration \texttt{000} is the native
forward pass. By Proposition~\ref{prop:single}, \texttt{001} to \texttt{011} give
the same result as \texttt{000} on every example, and \texttt{101} the same as
\texttt{100} (Table~\ref{tab:routing} in the appendix). With IDF on, mean MMLU accuracy
falls from $0.480$ to between $0.382$ and $0.390$, and WikiText perplexity rises from
$7.49$ to $7.86$ or $7.88$. All-on is worse than all-off on 52 subjects and better on 3,
and significantly worse after Holm correction in 22 of the 58 rows (57 subjects and
WikiText). IDF sends tokens towards experts the router rarely chose during calibration. The frequency bias loses less (MMLU $0.428$, perplexity $7.73$). The frequency-curve predictor
predicts $m$ of $2.05$ to $2.18$ for every subject, right in sign on 3 of the 55 subjects with a
nonzero margin ($0.05$) and wrong on WikiText, and its MAE is $3.98$ against the limit of
$1.81$. No label-free rule was registered for routing, because its
planned reference, a mixture over all 64 experts, was not implemented.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\paragraph{Saturation.} On sparse codes derived from E5, saturation gives most of BM25's
gain without collection statistics, and $\mathrm{cv}_x$ ranks its effect at held-out
values of $k_1$. Where each item carries a single score and IDF is off,
saturation cannot change the selection up to ties (Proposition~\ref{prop:single}), and in
KV selection and routing it changed task scores almost nowhere.

\paragraph{IDF and length normalisation.} BM25 without IDF beats all-on at every support
budget but 16/64. Whether IDF and length normalisation help a code
on a collection is harder to say. The frequency curve does not predict it, and neither do
index statistics. Agreement with text BM25 helps a fitted model, but the label-free rule
built on it is no better than a constant in sign on new E5 rows and fails its registered
test on SPLADE-v3, where agreement favours configurations that behave like BM25. Dense E5, the
secondary reference, met both pass marks there, over only 10 collections and with an
interval for its gain that includes zero.

\paragraph{Frequency inside the model.} With frequency from the selector's own choices, IDF
down-weights the items the selector picks often, and accuracy falls in KV selection on two
models and in expert routing. In KV selection exact attention mass shows this without
labels. The rule built on it chooses as well as the oracle, as does always choosing
\texttt{010}. No row has $G > 0$, so its registered sign test cannot be passed, and
$\tilde{G}$ does not track the size of $G$.

\section*{Challenges, Limitations and Future Work}
\label{sec:limitations}

One encoder underlies every retrieval code, MIRACL is in E5's training data, and SPLADE is one
model. The KV runs use one 4K context and 100 examples per task, not the planned 500.
Variable tracking ran without RULER's answer prefix. Llama's full-attention answer is
empty on 362 of $1{,}300$ examples, all 100 of the first single-needle task among them, so
its mass reference covers 938. Routing uses one model. A frequency counted over unrelated prompts is the next
test.

\paragraph{Shuffled and uniform frequencies.} On ArguAna, NFCorpus and SciFact we replaced the real frequencies in two ways, over 42 rows
each. With shuffled frequencies IDF's mean Shapley value turns negative, and IDF's Shapley value
with the real frequencies is larger in $83\%$ of rows (one-sided Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-6}$).
Uniform frequencies remove IDF altogether, and all-on nDCG@10 is
then $0.157$ against $0.147$ with the real frequencies ($p = 0.15$).

\paragraph{SPLADE-v3 by configuration.} Configuration \texttt{110} scores $0.528$ on
SPLADE-v3, and adding length normalisation (\texttt{111}) gives $0.509$, a drop of $0.019$.
Length normalisation's Shapley value, $-0.073$ (Table~\ref{tab:shapley}), is larger in
magnitude because it also
averages over \texttt{001} and \texttt{101}. These divide by length without saturation and
score $0.13$ below \texttt{000} and $0.12$ below \texttt{100}. Saturation's Shapley value
of $0.048$ comes from adding it to \texttt{001} and \texttt{101}. Added to \texttt{000} or
\texttt{100}, it changes mean nDCG@10 by less than $0.01$.
